analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas leasing in waters off Florida's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from offering any tract for oil and gas leasing or preleasing in three areas: the Eastern Gulf of Mexico covered by the 2006 Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, the part of the South Atlantic Planning Area south of 30°43' North latitude, and the Straits of Florida Planning Area. It would not cancel leases already issued. The bill never moved past referral to committee and a subcommittee, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida coastal residents, beach tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fisheries, who are exposed to the risk of oil spills from offshore drilling. Permanent protection would also lock in the existing drilling exclusion in the Eastern Gulf rather than leaving it to expire or be renegotiated.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Secretary from offering any tract for oil and gas leasing or preleasing in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico area defined by the 2006 Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, the South Atlantic Planning Area south of 30°43' North latitude, and the Straits of Florida Planning Area [S2] [S3].

By writing the exclusion directly into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, the bill would make it harder for future administrations to open those waters to drilling, beyond the protection then in place under the 2006 law [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential drilling tracts in the Eastern Gulf and off south Florida, and the federal government would forgo any leasing revenue and royalties those tracts could have produced. Energy consumers could see a marginal effect from a smaller pool of domestic offshore acreage, though these areas were already mostly closed to new leasing under existing law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers seeking Gulf acreage

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently remove federal waters from energy production that could supply domestic oil and gas and generate federal royalties shared with Gulf states [S3].

It would add a statutory bar on tracts that were already largely protected by the moratorium in the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006, so its practical effect was mainly to make that protection permanent rather than to newly close open waters [S2].
The bill does not affect any rights under leases issued before enactment, so drilling could continue on pre-existing leases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to Florida's coastal economy and environment is real but the bill's incremental effect was modest, since the 2006 Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act already placed a drilling moratorium over most of the same Eastern Gulf waters. The main cost falls on oil and gas companies and federal royalty revenue, which is a small share of national production. The bill was narrow and, in practical terms, mostly a permanence measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then sent to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the Florida Coastal Protection Act on April 20, 2015 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S5].
On May 7, 2015, it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 114th Congress [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies interested in Eastern Gulf and South Atlantic drilling are better off, since the waters remain available to future leasing decisions rather than permanently closed by statute, as under the 2006 moratorium that can be revised by later law.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled in the 114th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. A single Democrat sponsored it with no cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-run Natural Resources Committee never acted on it, so any partisan split can only be inferred, not measured.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar new leasing in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico and waters off south Florida, removing acreage these companies could otherwise lease and drill. Their gain from access comes at the cost of spill risk borne by coastal residents and tourism.

industries.industry: Florida beach tourism and coastal fishing
industries.note: Keeping drilling out of the Eastern Gulf and the Straits of Florida protects beaches and fisheries that anchor Florida's coastal economy. A spill in those waters would hit these industries first.
